sentences: Two richly dressed men stand at full length in front of a green curtain.
Between them, a two-tiered stand is crowded with globes, books and instruments.
And across the floor at their feet lies a strange, stretched shape that, at first glance, makes no sense at all.
This is The Ambassadors, painted in London in 1533 by Hans Holbein the Younger, so called to distinguish him from his father, also a painter.
It is oil on oak panels, slightly more than two metres high and two metres wide.
Holbein was born in Augsburg and spent his early career in Basel.
He first went to England in 1526, returned to settle there in 1532, and within a few years had become court painter to King Henry the Eighth.
On the left is Jean de Dinteville, the French ambassador; an inscription on his dagger sheath gives his age as twenty-nine.
On the right is his friend Georges de Selve, Bishop of Lavaur.
The book under his elbow tells us that he is twenty-five.
Now look at the upper shelf.
Here are a celestial globe, several kinds of sundial and other instruments for measuring the heavens.
These were rare and costly tools for telling time and tracking the stars, and they show two men at home in the learning of their age.
The lower shelf holds earthly things.
A terrestrial globe marks Polisy, Dinteville's home in France.
An arithmetic book lies open at the page on division.
The lute has one broken string, and a case of flutes is missing one.
These details are often read as signs of discord.
That year Henry the Eighth married Anne Boleyn in defiance of the Pope, and Europe was divided by religious conflict.
Beside the lute lies an open Lutheran hymnbook.
Now return to the shape on the floor.
From the front it is hard to read.
But stand close to the right-hand side and look along the surface at a sharp angle, and it turns into a human skull.
It is a reminder of death, and a brilliant display of the painter's skill.
Look also at the top left corner, where the curtain is pulled slightly aside.
A small silver crucifix is half hidden there.
It quietly points to the hope of salvation beyond the death that waits on the floor below.
The painting probably travelled home with Dinteville to his family château in France, and later passed through several owners.
The National Gallery in London bought it in 1890, and it has remained there ever since.
Step back and see the whole picture.
Youth, learning and wealth fill the panel, and right through the middle of it all runs a skull.
Today, try looking at something familiar from a slightly different angle, and see what quietly appears.
